missions.name: Puritan missions to Native Americans (John Eliot, the Mayhews, David Brainerd)
missions.statusNote: The colonial Puritan missions ended as an organised enterprise in the late eighteenth century (the last Mayhew missionary, Zachariah, died in 1806), but they left Native Christian congregations, notably among the Wampanoag of Martha's Vineyard and Mashpee and the Brothertown and Stockbridge-Munsee communities, that survive in transformed, Native-led form, and their literature shaped all later Anglo-American Protestant missions.
missions.summary: The first sustained English Protestant missions in the Americas, carried out by New England Puritans among the Algonquian peoples of Massachusetts, Martha's Vineyard and Plymouth from the 1640s, and continued in the eighteenth century by evangelical Presbyterians and Congregationalists such as David Brainerd among the Lenape and Eleazar Wheelock and the Mohegan minister Samson Occom. They produced the first Bible printed in the Americas, a network of 'praying towns' and a body of Native Christian leadership, but were inseparable from colonial land-taking and collapsed in the violence of King Philip's War (1675–76).
missions.story:
Massachusetts Bay's 1629 charter named the conversion of the Native peoples as a principal aim, and its seal showed an Indian saying 'Come over and help us', yet for more than a decade little was done. The first sustained work began on Martha's Vineyard, where Thomas Mayhew Jr, son of the island's proprietor, began instructing the Wampanoag Hiacoomes in 1643. On the mainland John Eliot, minister at Roxbury, learned Massachusett from a captive Montaukett interpreter, Cockenoe, and on 28 October 1646 preached his first sermon in the language at Nonantum, the wigwam of the sachem Waban near present-day Newton.

Eliot's English supporters published a series of promotional pamphlets (the so-called Eliot Tracts), and in 1649 the English Parliament chartered the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in New England (the New England Company), the first Protestant missionary corporation. With its funds Eliot founded the 'praying town' of Natick in 1651, a self-governing Native settlement organised on the model of Exodus 18 with rulers of hundreds and of tens, English-style houses, a meeting-house and a school. By 1674 the colonial superintendent Daniel Gookin counted fourteen praying towns in Massachusetts Bay with about 1,100 inhabitants, while further congregations existed in Plymouth Colony (Richard Bourne's church at Mashpee, gathered in 1670), on Nantucket and on Martha's Vineyard, where the first fully Native church was organised in 1670 with Hiacoomes and John Tackanash as its ministers.

Translation was the movement's great achievement. With Native collaborators, above all Cockenoe, John Sassamon, Job Nesutan and the printer James Printer (Wowaus), Eliot produced a Massachusett New Testament (1661) and complete Bible (1663), Mamusse Wunneetupanatamwe Up-Biblum God, printed at Cambridge, Massachusetts; it was the first Bible of any kind printed in the Western Hemisphere. Primers, catechisms, a grammar (1666) and devotional works followed, and Native literacy in the Vineyard and Mashpee communities was high enough that Wampanoag people kept deeds, wills and church records in their own language into the eighteenth century. Harvard opened an Indian College in 1655; Caleb Cheeshahteaumuck of the Vineyard graduated in 1665, though he died within a year.

The war of 1675–76 between the colonies and the Wampanoag sachem Metacom (King Philip) was a catastrophe for the mission. It was triggered in part by the death of the Christian Native John Sassamon, who had warned Plymouth of Metacom's plans. Distrusted by both sides, the mainland praying Indians were rounded up and interned on Deer Island in Boston Harbour in the winter of 1675–76, where many died of cold, hunger and disease; others were killed by colonial vigilantes or sold into slavery after the war despite Eliot's protests. Only four of the mainland praying towns were re-established, and Eliot, who revised his Bible in 1685, died in 1690 with his project in ruins. The Martha's Vineyard Wampanoag, by contrast, stayed neutral, and five generations of Mayhews ministered there until 1806; Experience Mayhew's Indian Converts (1727) recorded the lives of over a hundred Native Christian men, women and children.

In the eighteenth century the Great Awakening revived the cause. The Scottish Society for Propagating Christian Knowledge (SSPCK) commissioned David Brainerd, expelled from Yale, who worked at Kaunaumeek (New York) in 1743–44, at the Forks of the Delaware in Pennsylvania from 1744, and among the Lenape at Crossweeksung, New Jersey, where a revival in 1745–46 produced a Christian community that moved to Cranbury. Assisted by the Lenape interpreter Moses Tunda Tatamy, Brainerd also made long journeys to the Susquehanna. He died of tuberculosis in Jonathan Edwards's house at Northampton in October 1747, aged 29, and Edwards's edition of his diary (1749) became one of the most influential missionary books ever printed, read by William Carey, Henry Martyn and generations of later missionaries. John Sergeant (from 1735) and then Edwards himself (1751–58) served the Mahican mission town of Stockbridge.

Eleazar Wheelock's Moor's Indian Charity School at Lebanon, Connecticut (1754) trained Native and white missionaries. Its most famous product, the Mohegan Samson Occom, ordained by the Presbyterian Long Island presbytery in 1759, toured Britain in 1766–68 and raised about £12,000, which Wheelock used largely to found Dartmouth College (1769) for English students, leaving Occom feeling betrayed. Occom and his son-in-law Joseph Johnson then led Christian Algonquians from several New England communities to found Brothertown on Oneida land in New York in 1785, a Native-led Christian polity that later moved to Wisconsin.

The Puritan missions thus left a mixed legacy: genuine linguistic scholarship and Native Christian communities that endured, alongside a model in which conversion meant adopting English 'civility', missions served colonial land acquisition, and Christian Natives were among the worst sufferers of colonial war. Their texts, especially the lives of Eliot and Brainerd, became founding narratives for the British and American missionary societies of the 1790s and 1810s.
beliefs: Reformed (Calvinist) theology: salvation by God's sovereign grace through faith, with the preaching of the Word as the ordinary means of conversion.
Conviction that the gospel must be heard in the hearers' own language, which demanded Bible translation and Native literacy.

A strong expectation, fuelled by millennial speculation (some, including Eliot, entertained the idea that Native Americans descended from the lost tribes of Israel), that the conversion of the nations would precede Christ's kingdom.
Belief that true conversion should be accompanied by 'civility': settled agriculture, English dress, hairstyles, family order and Sabbath-keeping.
In the eighteenth-century phase, the Awakening's emphasis on a felt experience of new birth, as recorded in Brainerd's journals of the Crossweeksung revival.
Gathered-church ecclesiology: membership required a credible public testimony of conversion, so full Native church membership was granted slowly.
strategies: Preaching in Massachusett and other Algonquian languages after language study with Native interpreters such as Cockenoe and John Sassamon.
Founding segregated, self-governing 'praying towns' (Natick 1651 and later fourteen in Massachusetts Bay) with Native magistrates under colonial law.
Translation and printing: the Massachusett Bible (1663, revised 1685), primers, catechisms, Baxter's Call to the Unconverted and an Indian Grammar.
Training Native teachers and ministers, from Hiacoomes and John Tackanash on Martha's Vineyard to Samson Occom and the graduates of Wheelock's school.
Transatlantic fundraising through the New England Company (1649) and later the SSPCK, sustained by printed accounts of converts.
Itinerant evangelism in the Awakening style, with interpreters, as practised by Brainerd among the Lenape in New Jersey and Pennsylvania.
groupsReached: Massachusett and Nipmuc communities of eastern and central Massachusetts (Natick, Punkapoag, Hassanamesit and other praying towns).
Wampanoag of Martha's Vineyard, Nantucket and Mashpee on Cape Cod.
Lenape (Delaware) of New Jersey and the Forks of the Delaware.
Mahican (Stockbridge) people of western Massachusetts.
Mohegan, Pequot, Montaukett and other southern New England Algonquians associated with Occom and the Brothertown movement.
challenges: Few English ministers ever learned Native languages; the work depended on a handful of missionaries and Native interpreters.
Suspicion from sachems and powwows (shamans), who rightly saw the praying towns as eroding their authority and land base.
Distrust and hostility from colonists who coveted Native land and regarded all Natives as enemies in wartime.
Epidemic disease, which devastated Native populations before and during the mission period.
King Philip's War (1675–76), which destroyed most of the mainland praying towns and the trust on which the mission rested.
Chronic dependence on English funding and on the colonial government's goodwill.
harms: Conversion was tied to cultural renunciation: Eliot's 1646 rules for praying Indians at Concord prohibited long hair, traditional mourning practices and other customs.
Praying towns concentrated Native people on reduced land, which in practice eased English acquisition of the rest of their territory.
During King Philip's War Christian Natives were interned on Deer Island, where many died, and some were sold into Caribbean slavery afterward.
Missionary tracts exaggerated success for English donors, and the New England Company's funds were sometimes diverted to English purposes.
Funds raised by Samson Occom for Native education were used largely to found Dartmouth College for white students.
Colonial guardianship of praying towns and later Native 'plantations' left communities under paternalistic overseers well into the nineteenth century.
developments: The Massachusett Bible of 1663, the first Bible printed in the Americas and a landmark of vernacular translation.
Native Christian congregations, particularly among the Wampanoag of Aquinnah and Mashpee, that remained Native-led into modern times.
A tradition of Native literacy in Algonquian languages; Wampanoag documents later helped the twentieth-century revival of the Wôpanâak language.
Native Christian leaders and writers such as Hiacoomes, James Printer, Samson Occom and Joseph Johnson.
The New England Company (1649), the first Protestant missionary corporation, which still exists as a charity.
Edwards's Life of Brainerd (1749), which inspired William Carey, Henry Martyn and much of the modern missionary movement.
missions.outcome: As a colonial project the Puritan mission largely failed: King Philip's War destroyed most of Eliot's praying towns, and later efforts reached only small communities. Yet Native Christian congregations survived on Martha's Vineyard, at Mashpee, Stockbridge and Brothertown, and the movement's literature, especially Eliot's Bible and Brainerd's diary, gave the later evangelical missionary movement its models and heroes.

countries.country: Massachusetts Bay Colony (Natick and the praying towns)
countries.text: Eliot preached at Nonantum in 1646 and founded Natick in 1651; fourteen praying towns existed by 1674 before King Philip's War destroyed most of them.
The Mayhew family's mission among the Wampanoag produced the first Native church (1670) and a lasting, largely Native-led Christian community at Aquinnah (Gay Head).
Richard Bourne ministered to the Wampanoag of Mashpee on Cape Cod, where a Native church was gathered in 1670; the Mashpee Old Indian Meetinghouse dates from 1684.
Wheelock's Moor's Charity School trained Native pupils, and Samson Occom ministered among the Mohegan and other southern New England peoples.
Brainerd's preaching produced a Lenape revival in 1745–46 and a Christian community that his brother John Brainerd later led, eventually at Brotherton (Indian Mills), New Jersey's first reservation.

countries.country: Pennsylvania (Forks of the Delaware and Susquehanna)
countries.text: Brainerd worked among the Lenape near present-day Easton and made several journeys to Shamokin and other Susquehanna towns with his interpreter Moses Tatamy.
John Sergeant and later Jonathan Edwards served the Mahican mission town of Stockbridge, whose people later moved west as the Stockbridge-Munsee nation.
Occom and Joseph Johnson led Christian Algonquians from New England to found Brothertown on Oneida land; the community later relocated to Wisconsin in the 1830s.

journeys.title: David Brainerd's mission journeys among the Mahican and Lenape (1743–1747)
journeys.people: David Brainerd, with interpreter Moses Tunda Tatamy
journeys.text: Commissioned by the SSPCK, Brainerd spent a lonely year among the Mahicans at Kaunaumeek, moved to the Lenape at the Forks of the Delaware, made exhausting horseback journeys to the Susquehanna, and saw a revival among the Lenape at Crossweeksung in 1745–46, settling the converts at Cranbury. Sick with tuberculosis, he rode to Jonathan Edwards's home in Northampton, where he died on 9 October 1747.

journeys.title: Samson Occom's fundraising tour of Britain (1765–1768)
journeys.people: Samson Occom and Nathaniel Whitaker
journeys.text: Occom preached some 300 sermons in England and Scotland, met George Whitefield and the Earl of Dartmouth, and raised about £12,000 for Wheelock's school. On his return he found his family impoverished and the money directed to Dartmouth College, a breach that turned him toward a Native-led Christian future at Brothertown.

relations.text: New England Congregationalists who founded the American Board in 1810 saw themselves as heirs of Eliot and Brainerd, and the Board's early missions to the Cherokee and Choctaw continued the Native American mission.
Carey's Enquiry (1792) cited Eliot and Brainerd as proof that missions were possible, and Brainerd's Life shaped the spirituality of the first British missionaries.

agreements.text: Cotton Mather corresponded with A. H. Francke and with Ziegenbalg in Tranquebar, and both movements shared a commitment to vernacular Bibles, catechising and schools.
Both worked among the Mahican and Lenape and valued experiential conversion, though they rarely cooperated in practice.

disagreements.text: Puritans defined their mission against Spanish Catholic missions, which they condemned for forced baptisms and cruelty, while their own mission was likewise bound up with conquest.
New England and New York authorities distrusted Moravian missionaries as suspected papists or French agents, and in 1744 New York expelled them from Shekomeko.

deviations: Although converting the Native peoples was a stated purpose of the Massachusetts charter, the colony did almost nothing for its first fifteen years and later used praying towns as instruments of land control.
The insistence on English 'civility' before full church membership departed from the Reformed principle that faith alone, not culture, qualifies for the church.
Wheelock's redirection of Native-raised funds to an English college betrayed the stated purpose of the Indian charity school.

missions.name: Danish-Halle Mission (Ziegenbalg, Plütschau, Schwartz)

origin.name: Copenhagen (royal Mission College) and Halle (Francke Foundations)

missions.statusNote: The Danish-Halle enterprise faded in the early nineteenth century as Halle Pietism gave way to rationalism and Denmark sold Tranquebar to Britain (1845). Its congregations passed to the SPCK and SPG and, at Tranquebar, to the Leipzig Mission (1847), from which the Tamil Evangelical Lutheran Church (TELC) emerged in 1919; other descendants are now in the Church of South India.
missions.summary: The first organised Protestant mission in India, begun in 1706 when two German Pietists from Halle, Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plütschau, landed at the Danish trading colony of Tranquebar (Tharangambadi) on the Tamil coast under the patronage of King Frederick IV of Denmark. Combining Lutheran orthodoxy with Halle Pietism, it pioneered Tamil Bible translation, printing, schools, the study of Hindu religion and an ordained Indian ministry, and through Christian Friedrich Schwartz extended into Thanjavur and Tirunelveli. It also kept caste distinctions inside its churches, a choice that remained contested for two centuries.
missions.story:
Frederick IV of Denmark, influenced by his Pietist court chaplain Franz Julius Lütkens, resolved in 1704 to send missionaries to the Danish East India Company's small colony at Tranquebar, acquired in 1620. No Danish candidates could be found, so Lütkens turned to August Hermann Francke's foundations at Halle, whose students combined academic theology with a disciplined piety and practical training. Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg (b. 1682) and Heinrich Plütschau (b. 1676) were ordained in Copenhagen, sailed on the Sophia Hedwig on 29 November 1705, and landed at Tranquebar on 9 July 1706, the beginning of continuous Protestant mission in Asia.

The colony's commandant and chaplains, who had not been consulted, were hostile; Ziegenbalg was imprisoned for four months in 1708–09. Nevertheless he learned Tamil by sitting with children in a village school, collected and read palm-leaf manuscripts, and wrote extensively on Tamil religion and society, including the Genealogy of the Malabarian Gods (1713), which Halle refused to print on the grounds that missionaries were sent to root out heathenism, not to spread it in Europe; it appeared only in 1867. The first baptisms took place in May 1707, and the Jerusalem Church was built in the same year, replaced by the larger New Jerusalem Church in 1718. With a press sent by the English Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge (SPCK) in 1712 and Tamil type cast at Halle, the mission printed the Tamil New Testament (1714–15), the first New Testament printed in any Indian language, as well as catechisms, hymn books and a Tamil grammar (1716).

Ziegenbalg returned to Europe in 1714–16, where he was received by George I in London and visited Halle (where the boy Count Zinzendorf, a pupil at Francke's school, met him), and married. Worn out, he died at Tranquebar on 23 February 1719, aged 36, by which time the congregation numbered roughly 250. Benjamin Schultze continued the translation of the Old Testament and in 1726 moved to Madras, where from 1728 he led the SPCK's 'English Mission' staffed by Halle Lutherans; further stations followed at Cuddalore (1737) and Trichinopoly (1762). The Danish king's Mission College in Copenhagen (1714) also sponsored Hans Egede's mission to Greenland (1721). In 1733 the mission ordained its first Tamil pastor, Aaron, a landmark in the formation of an indigenous ministry.

The outstanding figure of the second generation was Christian Friedrich Schwartz (1726–1798), who arrived in 1750 and spent 48 years in South India without returning home. Based at Trichinopoly and from 1778 at Thanjavur (Tanjore), he became confidant of Raja Tulaja, guardian of the young Serfoji II, interpreter and envoy for the East India Company (including a mission to Hyder Ali at Seringapatam in 1779) and the founder of schools for Indians and Europeans. He baptised the Brahmin widow Clorinda, who built the first church at Palayamkottai in 1785, and his catechist Sathyanathan was ordained in 1790 to lead the growing Tirunelveli congregations. The poet Vedanayagam Sastriar, a Schwartz convert, created a Tamil Christian literature and music. Serfoji II raised a marble memorial to Schwartz in the Thanjavur church.

The Halle Reports (Hallesche Berichte, published from 1710) made Tranquebar known across Protestant Europe and colonial America; Cotton Mather corresponded with Ziegenbalg, the Wesleys' father Samuel admired the mission, and the reports were a direct inspiration for the Moravians and later the Baptist and London missionary societies. Johann Philipp Fabricius in Madras produced a revised Tamil Bible and hymnal that remained standard for over a century.

From the 1780s the mission declined: Halle drifted toward Enlightenment rationalism and sent few recruits, funds dried up during the Napoleonic wars, and the remaining missionaries were elderly. Anglican bishops of Calcutta and Madras, notably Daniel Wilson in 1833, demanded that former Lutheran congregations abandon caste distinctions at worship, provoking secessions. In 1825–26 the SPCK transferred its stations to the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel, Denmark sold Tranquebar to Britain in 1845, and the Leipzig Evangelical Lutheran Mission took over the Tranquebar work in 1847, its director Karl Graul again defending toleration of caste as a social rather than religious matter. The Tamil Evangelical Lutheran Church, constituted in 1919 with its seat at Tranquebar, is the direct heir.
beliefs: Lutheran confessional theology (justification by faith, Word and sacraments) combined with Halle Pietism's stress on conversion, personal holiness and practical charity.
Conviction, derived from Spener and Francke, that every Christian should read Scripture, so that translation, literacy and schooling were essential to mission.
Belief that understanding the religion of the hearers was necessary for persuasion, which led Ziegenbalg to serious (if polemical) study of Tamil Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava texts.
Expectation that converts would form a self-sustaining Indian church with ordained Indian pastors, at least in principle.
A view of caste, prevailing for much of the mission's history, as a civil institution that could be tolerated within the church rather than a religious system to be abolished.
strategies: Mastery of Tamil (and Portuguese, the colonial lingua franca), with grammars, dictionaries and the study of Tamil literature.
Bible translation and printing: the Tamil New Testament of 1714–15, the first printed in an Indian language, and Fabricius's later revision.
Schools for boys and girls, charity schools, a seminary for catechists, and Schwartz's schools at Thanjavur, Ramnad and Shivaganga.
Training and ordaining Indian catechists and pastors (Aaron 1733, Diogo 1741, Sathyanathan 1790).
Cooperation across confessions and nations: Danish royal sponsorship, German missionaries and English SPCK funding and printing.
Publication of detailed mission reports (Hallesche Berichte) to build European support and prayer.
groupsReached: Tamil-speaking Hindus of Tranquebar and the Kaveri delta, especially Vellalar and other Sudra castes and Paraiyar labourers.
Portuguese-speaking Eurasians, Catholic converts and enslaved people in the Danish and British coastal settlements.
Converts in Thanjavur, Trichinopoly and the Tirunelveli country through Schwartz and his catechists, including Shanar (Nadar) villages in the south.
British soldiers and Company servants, to whom Schwartz and others ministered as SPCK chaplains.
challenges: Opposition from Danish colonial officials and chaplains who feared commercial disruption, including Ziegenbalg's imprisonment in 1708–09.
A tiny number of missionaries, high mortality and long, slow communications with Europe.
Rivalry and polemic with Jesuit and other Catholic missions already established in the Tamil country.
Caste: high-caste converts refused to share church seating or the communion cup with Paraiyar converts, while lower-caste converts resented the distinctions.
Decline of Halle Pietism under rationalism after c. 1780 and the drying-up of recruits and funds.
War and political upheaval in the Carnatic, including the Anglo-Mysore wars.
harms: Separate seating, separate communion order and other caste distinctions were tolerated in Lutheran congregations, entrenching discrimination against Dalit Christians.
Ziegenbalg's and his successors' writings, though pioneering, framed Hindu religion largely as idolatry to be overcome, and Halle suppressed his more sympathetic ethnography.
Dependence on colonial power: Schwartz served as a diplomat and agent for the East India Company, blurring the line between mission and empire.
Converts often lost family, livelihood and inheritance and became dependent on mission employment.
developments: The first printed Bible portions in any Indian language and pioneering Tamil printing at Tranquebar.
Early Protestant ordination of Indian clergy and a tradition of Tamil Christian poetry and hymnody (Vedanayagam Sastriar).
Serious European scholarship on Tamil language and religion, a forerunner of Indology.
Schools, including early schooling for girls, and the educational reforms of Schwartz's era at Thanjavur.
A model of international, interconfessional mission sponsorship that inspired the Moravians and the British societies of the 1790s.
Congregations that survive in the Tamil Evangelical Lutheran Church and the Church of South India.
missions.outcome: The mission planted the first Protestant churches in India and set the pattern of translation, printing, schools and indigenous clergy that later missions adopted. Its institutional life ended with Danish withdrawal in 1845, but its congregations continue in the Tamil Evangelical Lutheran Church (1919) and in the Church of South India, and Ziegenbalg is honoured in Tamil Nadu as a pioneer of Tamil printing.

Benjamin Schultze founded the SPCK-funded 'English Mission' at Madras, later led by Fabricius.
SPCK mission staffed by Halle missionaries, briefly the base of Schwartz on his arrival in 1750.
Schwartz's base, with a church for the British garrison and Tamil congregations.
Schwartz's later base at the Maratha court, with schools and Christ Church in the fort.
Congregations among Vellalar and Shanar villagers led by Clorinda, Sathyanathan and other catechists, the seed of later mass movements.
The king and the Mission College (Collegium de cursu Evangelii promovendo, 1714) in Copenhagen sponsored the mission and Egede's Greenland mission.

Hans Egede, a Norwegian Lutheran pastor backed by the Danish crown and Mission College, began work at Godthåb (Nuuk).

journeys.title: Ziegenbalg and Plütschau's voyage to Tranquebar (1705–1706)
journeys.people: Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plütschau
journeys.text: After ordination in Copenhagen the two Halle-trained missionaries sailed on 29 November 1705 aboard the Sophia Hedwig, rounded the Cape of Good Hope and reached Tranquebar on 9 July 1706, where the Danish commandant at first refused to help them.

journeys.title: Christian Friedrich Schwartz's journey and career in South India (1749–1798)
journeys.people: Christian Friedrich Schwartz
journeys.text: Schwartz sailed via London to Cuddalore in July 1750 and worked at Tranquebar until moving to Trichinopoly in 1762 and Thanjavur in 1778; in 1779 he travelled to Seringapatam as an envoy of the Madras government to Hyder Ali, who trusted him. He died at Thanjavur in 1798 without ever returning to Europe.

relations.text: Zinzendorf, educated at Halle, met Ziegenbalg in 1715 and later drew on the Danish connection (Copenhagen, Egede's Greenland and the Danish West Indies) for the first Moravian missions.
Carey's Enquiry cited the Danish mission, and Serampore, the BMS base from 1800, was a Danish settlement whose authorities protected the Baptists as Tranquebar's had protected the Lutherans.

agreements.text: Both put Bible translation, printing, schools and the study of Indian languages and literature at the centre of mission.
Through the Francke–Mather correspondence the two shared a Protestant vision of vernacular Scripture and catechised Christian communities.

disagreements.text: Ziegenbalg and his successors disputed with Jesuit missionaries in the Tamil country and criticised their accommodation of Hindu customs, even while Lutheran congregations themselves accommodated caste.

Evangelical Anglicans, notably Bishop Daniel Wilson of Calcutta (1833), demanded the abolition of caste distinctions in the former Lutheran congregations, which the Lutheran tradition, later through the Leipzig Mission, resisted.

deviations: Halle's Pietist mission increasingly accommodated caste within the church, in tension with its own teaching on the equality of believers at the Lord's Table.
From the 1780s Halle's theological drift toward rationalism undercut the mission's original Pietist conviction and starved it of recruits.
Schwartz's role as a political envoy and adviser to the East India Company went beyond the mission's founding brief.

missions.name: Moravian missions (Herrnhut, Zinzendorf, Dober, Greenland, Caribbean, Suriname)
missions.statusNote: The Moravian Church (Unitas Fratrum) continues as a worldwide communion of about a million members organised in self-governing provinces; the former mission fields now far outnumber the European and North American provinces, with the largest churches in Tanzania, the Caribbean, Suriname, South Africa and Nicaragua.
missions.summary: The first Protestant church to treat world mission as the task of the whole community. From the refugee settlement of Herrnhut on Count Zinzendorf's estate, lay artisans went out from 1732 to the enslaved Africans of the Danish West Indies, to Greenland, Suriname, South Africa, Native North America, Labrador, Jamaica and Antigua and eventually to Tibet, Australia, Nicaragua and East Africa. Preaching the suffering Saviour and supporting themselves by their trades, they built enduring Afro-Caribbean and Indigenous churches, while also accepting, and in places practising, slaveholding.
missions.story:
Herrnhut was founded in 1722 by Protestant refugees from Moravia, some descended from the old Unity of the Brethren (Unitas Fratrum), who settled on the Berthelsdorf estate of Count Nicolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf. After a eucharistic experience of reconciliation on 13 August 1727 the community organised itself into 'choirs', adopted a round-the-clock prayer watch that continued for about a hundred years, and developed an intense devotion to the wounded Lamb of God. Zinzendorf, raised in Halle Pietism, had as a schoolboy formed the 'Order of the Mustard Seed' to spread the gospel and had met the Tranquebar missionary Ziegenbalg.

In 1731, at the coronation of Christian VI in Copenhagen, Zinzendorf's servants met Anthony Ulrich, an enslaved man from the Danish island of St Thomas, and saw Inuit converts of Hans Egede's Greenland mission. Anthony's appeal moved two young men at Herrnhut: Leonhard Dober, a potter, and David Nitschmann, a carpenter. They left Herrnhut on 21 August 1732, walked to Copenhagen and arrived at St Thomas on 13 December 1732. The popular story that they meant to sell themselves into slavery rests on Dober's stated willingness to do so; it never happened. In 1733 Christian David and the cousins Matthäus and Christian Stach went to Greenland, where the first convert, Kajarnak, was baptised in 1739 and the settlement of Neu-Herrnhut grew beside Egede's Godthåb.

Within a decade the small community had sent workers to Suriname (1735), Georgia (1735), the Gold Coast and South Africa (1737), Lapland, Ceylon and the Arctic. On St Thomas the Afro-Caribbean freedwoman Rebecca Protten became a leading evangelist among the enslaved, and when she, her husband Matthäus Freundlich and others were imprisoned in 1738, Zinzendorf himself sailed to the island in 1739 to secure their release. In South Africa Georg Schmidt baptised Khoikhoi converts at Baviaanskloof from 1737 but was forced out in 1744 by Dutch Reformed clergy who disputed a lay missionary's right to baptise; the Moravians returned in 1792 and refounded the station as Genadendal. Antigua (1756) and Jamaica (1754) became major fields, and by the early nineteenth century Moravian congregations in the British and Danish Caribbean counted tens of thousands of members.

In North America the Moravians founded Bethlehem and Nazareth in Pennsylvania (1741) and Salem in North Carolina (1766), and from Shekomeko in New York (1740) built a Christian community among the Mahican and Lenape. David Zeisberger led Christian Lenape through repeated forced migrations to the Ohio country (Schoenbrunn and Gnadenhütten, 1772), where on 8 March 1782 Pennsylvania militia murdered 96 unarmed Christian Lenape men, women and children at Gnadenhütten. From 1771 the Brethren worked among the Inuit of Labrador at Nain, Okak and Hopedale.

The movement's distinctive methods impressed Protestants everywhere. Missionaries were usually craftsmen who earned their keep; they sought 'first-fruits' (individual converts gathered into disciplined settlements) rather than whole nations; they preached the blood and wounds of Christ before teaching about God the Creator; and decisions, including marriages and postings, were often made by lot. John Wesley met Moravians on his 1735 voyage to Georgia and was guided by Peter Böhler before his Aldersgate experience in 1738, and William Carey's Enquiry (1792) held up 'what these Moravians have done' as a rebuke to other churches. The British Society for the Furtherance of the Gospel (1741) supported the work from London.

Crises were frequent: the 'Sifting Time' of the 1740s brought extravagant devotional excess to Herrnhaag; Zinzendorf's debts nearly bankrupted the Unity in the 1750s; and after his death in 1760 the church became more cautious and institutional. Yet the missions kept spreading: to the Mosquito Coast of Nicaragua (1849), Victoria in Australia (1850), the Himalayas at Kyelang (1853) and Leh, where Heinrich August Jäschke compiled a Tibetan dictionary, Alaska (1885) and German East Africa (1891), today Tanzania. Emancipation in the Caribbean (1834–38) and Suriname (1863) transformed the plantation congregations into free churches, and in the twentieth century the provinces became autonomous members of a worldwide Unity governed by a Unity Synod.
beliefs: A 'theology of the heart' centred on the crucified Saviour, the Lamb whose blood and wounds bring salvation, expressed in hymns, litanies and daily texts (the Losungen, from 1731).
Conviction that the Holy Spirit was already preparing individuals among all peoples, so that missionaries should seek these 'first-fruits' rather than mass conversions.
Acceptance of the Augsburg Confession alongside a broadly ecumenical vision of the 'Unity of the Brethren' as a fellowship within and across churches.
Belief that the risen Christ is Chief Elder of the church (declared in 1741) and that his will could be discerned through prayer and the lot.
A spiritual, inward equality of believers that coexisted with acceptance of social hierarchy, including slavery, in this world.
strategies: Sending lay artisans (potters, carpenters, weavers) who supported themselves by trade and lived among the people.
Building disciplined Christian settlements (Neu-Herrnhut, Genadendal, Gnadenhütten, Nain) on the Herrnhut model, with choirs, schools and crafts.
Learning local languages and creoles, including Dutch Creole on St Thomas, Sranan in Suriname, Greenlandic, Inuktitut, Lenape and Miskito.
Training and appointing Black and Indigenous 'helpers' and elders, such as Rebecca Protten on St Thomas and the Lenape helpers in Ohio.
Intensive communication through diaries and reports circulated to all settlements (the Gemeinnachrichten), fostering a global church identity.
Long-term commitment: missionaries often served for life and were buried in mission graveyards (God's Acres).
groupsReached: Enslaved Africans and free people of colour in the Danish West Indies, Jamaica, Antigua, Barbados, St Kitts, Tobago and Suriname.
Inuit of Greenland and Labrador.
Khoikhoi and other peoples of the Cape (Genadendal, Elim, Mamre).
Mahican, Lenape (Delaware) and Cherokee communities in North America.
Miskito and other Caribbean coast peoples of Nicaragua and Honduras.
Nyakyusa, Safwa and other peoples of south-western Tanzania; Ladakhi and Lahauli Buddhists in the western Himalayas; Aboriginal Australians in Victoria and Queensland.
challenges: Extremely high mortality in the tropics: dozens of early missionaries to St Thomas, St Croix and Guinea died within months.
Opposition from planters, colonial clergy and governments, who feared literacy and Christian fellowship among the enslaved.
Persecution in Europe and America: the Brethren were expelled from Saxony (Zinzendorf exiled 1736–47) and suspected as papists, enthusiasts or French agents in the colonies.
Frontier violence in North America, culminating in the Gnadenhütten massacre of 1782.
Financial crisis in the 1750s caused by Zinzendorf's ambitious spending.
Very small home base: a church of a few thousand members sustained missions on several continents.
harms: The Moravians accepted slavery as an earthly order and preached obedience to masters; the mission itself owned enslaved people on St Thomas, in Suriname and at Salem in North Carolina.
Segregation and racial hierarchy in Moravian congregations, for example the segregated Salem congregation from the 1820s, contradicted their earlier mixed fellowship.
Closed mission settlements imposed detailed rules on Indigenous life and made converts dependent on mission land and trade.
In Greenland and Labrador the trading and settlement systems promoted by missions disrupted Inuit subsistence patterns and exposed communities to epidemic disease.
Moravian-run Aboriginal stations in Australia, such as Ebenezer and Ramahyuck, were part of the protection system that removed Aboriginal people from their land.
developments: The first sustained Protestant mission to enslaved Africans, which helped create Afro-Caribbean Christianity and Black church leadership.
The model of a whole church committed to mission; by the late eighteenth century the Moravians sent proportionally far more missionaries than any other Protestant body.
Linguistic work in Greenlandic, Inuktitut, Sranan, Miskito, Lenape and Tibetan, including Jäschke's Tibetan dictionary (1881).
Schools and teacher-training in the Caribbean and South Africa (Genadendal's teachers' college, 1838) that educated generations of free people of colour.
Decisive influence on John Wesley, William Carey and the British missionary societies of the 1790s.
Self-governing provinces today in Tanzania, the Caribbean, Suriname, South Africa, Nicaragua, Labrador, Alaska and elsewhere.
missions.outcome: From a refugee village of a few hundred people the Moravian missions produced a worldwide church whose members are now overwhelmingly African, Afro-Caribbean, Latin American and Indigenous. Their example of lay, self-supporting, lifelong mission and their influence on Wesley and Carey make them a hinge between Pietism and the modern Protestant missionary movement, while their accommodation of slavery remains a contested part of the record.

countries.country: Danish West Indies (St Thomas, St Croix, St John)
countries.text: First Moravian mission: Dober and Nitschmann on St Thomas, followed by congregations of thousands of enslaved Africans on all three islands.
Neu-Herrnhut beside Godthåb (Nuuk) and later stations; transferred to the Danish Lutheran church in 1900.
Work among enslaved Africans in Paramaribo and the plantations and among Maroons (Saramaka, from 1765); now one of the largest Moravian provinces.
Georg Schmidt at Baviaanskloof (1737–44); Genadendal refounded 1792, followed by Mamre, Elim and Eastern Cape stations.
Settlements at Bethlehem, Nazareth and Salem and missions to Mahican, Lenape and Cherokee peoples.
Mission on the estates of absentee planters; Moravian schools and congregations grew rapidly after emancipation.
One of the largest early fields, with thousands of members by 1800 and a strong tradition of Black lay leadership.
Jens Haven founded Nain among the Inuit; Okak, Hopedale and Hebron followed.
Mission among the Miskito and Creole population of Bluefields and Puerto Cabezas; revival in the 1880s made it a major province.
Mission at Kyelang (1853) and Leh (1885) in the western Himalayas, with Tibetan translation work by Jäschke.
Stations among Aboriginal people at Ebenezer (1859) and Ramahyuck in Victoria and later in Queensland.

Mission among the Yup'ik of the Kuskokwim region from Bethel.

journeys.title: Dober and Nitschmann to St Thomas (1732)
journeys.people: Leonhard Dober and David Nitschmann
journeys.text: Setting out on foot from Herrnhut on 21 August 1732 with little money, the two men walked to Copenhagen, where court officials helped them obtain passage on a Dutch ship that sailed on 8 October and reached St Thomas on 13 December 1732. Nitschmann returned in 1733; Dober stayed until 1734.

journeys.title: The first Moravian party to Greenland (1733)
journeys.people: Christian David, Matthäus Stach and Christian Stach
journeys.text: The party sailed from Copenhagen with royal permission and landed near Egede's colony in May 1733, founding Neu-Herrnhut. Years of failure ended when Kajarnak, a southern Greenlander, responded to Johann Beck's reading of the passion narrative in 1738 and was baptised in 1739.

journeys.title: Zinzendorf's visit to St Thomas (1738–1739)
journeys.people: Nicolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf
journeys.text: Arriving in January 1739 to find the missionaries Friedrich Martin and Matthäus and Rebecca Freundlich in prison, Zinzendorf secured their release, preached to large gatherings of enslaved people and, in a notorious sermon, urged them to obey their masters.

journeys.title: Georg Schmidt to the Cape (1736–1737)
journeys.people: Georg Schmidt
journeys.text: Sent with the support of Dutch Pietists, Schmidt reached the Cape in July 1737 and settled among the Khoikhoi in the Baviaanskloof valley, teaching, farming and eventually baptising five converts, which led to his recall in 1744.

journeys.title: Zeisberger and the Christian Lenape migrate to Ohio (1772–1782)
journeys.people: David Zeisberger, John Heckewelder and Christian Lenape
journeys.text: Pressed by settlers, the Christian Lenape moved from Pennsylvania to the Tuscarawas valley, founding Schoenbrunn and Gnadenhütten. During the Revolutionary War British-allied forces removed them to Sandusky; a group returned to harvest their crops and were massacred by Pennsylvania militia on 8 March 1782.

relations.text: Moravians shaped John Wesley through his voyage to Georgia (1735–36), Peter Böhler's counsel and the Fetter Lane society, and Wesley's visit to Herrnhut in 1738.
Carey's Enquiry (1792) cited the Moravians as the model of a small church in earnest about mission, and their Periodical Accounts were read at the BMS's founding meeting.
Moravian reports, promoted by the London Society for the Furtherance of the Gospel, helped inspire the evangelicals who founded the LMS in 1795.

agreements.text: Both stressed felt assurance of salvation, small-group discipline and hymn-singing, and both went to the enslaved Caribbean early.
Both drew on Halle Pietism and the Danish crown's colonies, and both prized translation and lifelong service.

disagreements.text: In 1740 Wesley broke with the Fetter Lane Moravians over 'stillness' (waiting for faith without using the means of grace) and later criticised Zinzendorf's antinomian tendencies.
Halle Pietists, especially Gotthilf August Francke, distrusted Zinzendorf's theology and independence and opposed Moravian work in Halle's sphere, including in India (the Nicobar mission of 1768–87).

deviations: The 'Sifting Time' (c. 1743–50) introduced extravagant blood-and-wounds devotion and spiritual excesses that Zinzendorf himself eventually condemned.
Early mixed-race fellowship on St Thomas and at Bethlehem gave way in the nineteenth century to segregated congregations in the American South.
From preaching spiritual equality the mission moved to owning enslaved people on its own plantations, contrary to the egalitarian impulse of its origins.

missions.name: Evangelical Revival and Methodist missions (Wesley, Whitefield, Coke, Asbury)

origin.name: London (Aldersgate and the Foundery) and Bristol

missions.statusNote: The British and American Methodist missionary societies have been absorbed into church agencies (the Methodist Church in Britain's World Church Relationships; the United Methodist General Board of Global Ministries), and almost all former mission fields are autonomous conferences. The World Methodist Council's member churches report around 80 million people, increasingly in Africa and Asia; American United Methodism divided in 2019–24, when about a quarter of US congregations left, many joining the Global Methodist Church.
missions.summary: The Evangelical Revival of the 1730s–40s, led by John and Charles Wesley and George Whitefield, created Methodism, a disciplined lay-led movement that treated 'the world as my parish'. Through itinerant preachers, class meetings and the missionary drive of Thomas Coke and Francis Asbury, Methodism spread across the American frontier, the Caribbean, West and Southern Africa, the South Pacific, India and East Asia, becoming one of the largest Protestant families and a seedbed of the Holiness and Pentecostal movements.
missions.story:
The revival grew from the 'Holy Club' at Oxford, where from 1729 John and Charles Wesley, George Whitefield and others pursued disciplined piety. John Wesley's failed mission as an SPG chaplain in Georgia (1735–37), where he met Moravian missionaries on the voyage, preceded his experience at a society meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, on 24 May 1738, when he felt his heart 'strangely warmed'. Whitefield, a spellbinding preacher, began open-air preaching to the miners of Kingswood near Bristol in February 1739 and persuaded Wesley to follow. Wesley declared in 1739 that he looked upon 'all the world as my parish', and for fifty years he rode some 250,000 miles organising societies, classes and bands across Britain and Ireland.

Whitefield crossed the Atlantic seven times and became the best-known figure of the Great Awakening in the American colonies, preaching from Georgia to New England in 1739–40 to crowds that sometimes reached tens of thousands; he died at Newburyport, Massachusetts, in 1770. Methodism proper reached America through Irish immigrants, Philip Embury and Barbara Heck in New York (1766) and Robert Strawbridge in Maryland. Wesley sent preachers from 1769, including Francis Asbury (1771), who stayed through the Revolution. After American independence Wesley ordained Thomas Coke as superintendent, and at the Christmas Conference in Baltimore in December 1784 the Methodist Episcopal Church was organised with Coke and Asbury as its superintendents (soon styled bishops). Circuit riders carried Methodism to the frontier, and by 1830 it was the largest denomination in the United States.

Coke, a Welsh Anglican clergyman, was Methodism's missionary strategist. His 1783–84 Plan of the Society for the Establishment of Missions among the Heathens anticipated Carey's Enquiry. In 1786, bound for Nova Scotia, his ship was driven by storms to Antigua, where he landed on Christmas Day; there the planter Nathaniel Gilbert had begun preaching to his slaves in 1759, enslaved women such as Sophia Campbell and Mary Alley had kept the society going, and the shipwright John Baxter was leading some 2,000 members. Coke left missionaries across the Caribbean, crossed the Atlantic eighteen times, and in 1813 persuaded the Conference to launch a mission to Asia. He died at sea on 3 May 1814; his companions landed in Bombay and established the Ceylon mission.

The Wesleyan Methodist Missionary Society, formed in 1813–18, became one of the largest British societies. Sierra Leone (1811) built on Black Loyalist Methodists who had settled there from Nova Scotia in 1792; Barnabas Shaw entered South Africa in 1816 and William Shaw led the mission among the Xhosa from 1823. Thomas Birch Freeman, the son of an African father and English mother, reached Kumasi in Asante in 1839 and Badagry and Abeokuta in Yorubaland in 1842. In the Pacific, Tonga (1822, firmly from 1826) became Methodist after the baptism of Taufa'ahau, later King George Tupou I, in 1831, and Fiji (1835) followed, with the chief Cakobau converting in 1854 and Tongan and Fijian teachers carrying the faith further to Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands. Missions also went to Madras (1817), China (1851) and later to Burma and Upper Burma.

American Methodism created its own Missionary Society in 1819. Melville Cox died within months of landing in Liberia in 1833 ('Let a thousand fall before Africa be given up'); William Butler began the North India mission at Bareilly in 1856, where Isabella Thoburn later founded the school that became Lucknow's Isabella Thoburn College; and Henry Appenzeller entered Korea in 1885. Black Methodist churches formed in protest at discrimination: the African Methodist Episcopal Church under Richard Allen (1816), which sent missionaries to Haiti, Sierra Leone and Liberia and in 1896 absorbed South Africa's Ethiopian Church, and the AME Zion Church.

Methodism repeatedly divided. Whitefield's Calvinist Methodists separated from Wesley's Arminians in 1741; British Methodism fractured into the Methodist New Connexion (1797), Primitive Methodists (1811), Bible Christians (1815) and others, each with missions, before reuniting in 1932. American Methodists split North and South over slavery in 1844 and reunited in 1939 (without the Black churches); the United Methodist Church was formed in 1968. Methodist teaching on Christian perfection fed the nineteenth-century Holiness movement and, through it, Pentecostalism, while Methodists such as John R. Mott were leading architects of the ecumenical movement. Former mission districts became autonomous conferences from the late nineteenth century onward, and today the churches of Africa, Asia, the Pacific and Latin America form the growing part of world Methodism.
beliefs: Arminian evangelical theology: Christ died for all, prevenient grace enables every person to respond, and 'all may be saved'.
The new birth and the witness of the Spirit, giving believers an assurance of salvation.
Christian perfection or entire sanctification: the possibility of perfect love toward God and neighbour in this life.
Social holiness: faith expressed in disciplined community and works of mercy, including Wesley's opposition to slavery (Thoughts upon Slavery, 1774) and to gin and smuggling.
The use of the 'means of grace' (prayer, Scripture, the Lord's Supper, fasting, Christian conference) as ordinary channels of God's grace.
A sense of urgency that the gospel should be offered to everyone, everywhere, expressed in Wesley's 'the world is my parish'.
strategies: Field preaching and itinerancy: preachers on horseback 'riding the circuit', from British market towns to the American frontier.
Class meetings of about twelve under a lay leader, bands and quarterly tickets, which gave converts discipline and pastoral care and let laypeople, including women and enslaved people, lead.
Lay preachers, local preachers and exhorters, including Black and women preachers in the early decades.
Hymn-singing: Charles Wesley's roughly 6,000 hymns carried theology to people who could not read.
Connexional organisation: an annual Conference that stationed preachers and directed resources across vast distances, adapted to mission districts overseas.
Schools, printing and later hospitals and colleges, especially in India, Africa, Korea and China.
Use of indigenous evangelists, notably Tongan and Fijian missionaries who carried Methodism across Melanesia.
groupsReached: Industrial workers, miners and the rural poor of Britain and Ireland.
Settlers and enslaved and free African Americans in North America, including the frontier and the slave South.
Enslaved and free people of colour in Antigua, the West Indies and Sierra Leone.
Fante and Asante in the Gold Coast, Yoruba and Egba in Nigeria, Xhosa, Mfengu and Sotho-Tswana in Southern Africa.
Tongans, Fijians and Samoans, and through Pacific teachers the peoples of New Britain, Papua and the Solomon Islands.
Tamil and Sinhala communities in Ceylon and South India, Hindi-speaking villages in North India, and Koreans, Chinese and Burmese.
challenges: Mob violence and clerical opposition in Britain in the 1740s, and hostility from planters in the Caribbean who feared Methodist preaching to the enslaved.
Tropical disease: West Africa was known as 'the white man's grave', and many early missionaries to Sierra Leone and the Gold Coast died within a year.
Tension between the Church of England and the Methodist societies, which led to separation after Wesley's death in 1791.
Slavery, which divided American Methodism in 1844 and compromised its early anti-slavery stance.
Repeated schisms over church government, lay rights and holiness teaching.
Theological liberalism and secularisation in the twentieth century, contributing to sharp decline in Britain and North America.
harms: Whitefield campaigned for the legalisation of slavery in Georgia (achieved in 1751) and owned enslaved people at his Bethesda orphanage.
American Methodism retreated from Wesley's anti-slavery rules, and Southern Methodism defended slavery and later segregation; Black Methodists were pushed into separate galleries and conferences.
Methodist missionaries in Fiji and Tonga were closely tied to chiefly power, and royal conversions brought coercive pressure on subjects.
Some missionaries endorsed colonial expansion, such as Wesleyans who supported British annexations in the Eastern Cape and Fiji (1874).
In Canada, Methodists ran Indian residential schools (later in the United Church of Canada), part of a system now recognised as causing grave harm to Indigenous children.
Paternalism in mission districts delayed autonomy for African and Asian churches well into the twentieth century.
developments: A mass lay movement that gave working people, women and Black Christians roles as leaders and preachers.
Charles Wesley's hymns and a congregational singing tradition now used across Protestantism.
Major contributions to education: Methodist schools and colleges across Africa, India and Korea, including Ewha (1886) and Isabella Thoburn College (1886).
Black church independence through the AME and AME Zion churches, central to African American religious and civil life.
Holiness teaching that gave rise to the Holiness churches, the Salvation Army and, indirectly, Pentecostalism.
Leadership in the ecumenical movement and social reform, including temperance, anti-slavery and later civil-rights activism.
missions.outcome: From a revival within the Church of England, Methodism became a worldwide family of churches of about 80 million people. Its mission societies have been absorbed into church agencies and its overseas districts are autonomous churches, many of them growing while Western Methodism declines and divides.

From New York and Maryland societies to the Methodist Episcopal Church (1784), the largest US denomination by 1830, plus the AME and AME Zion churches.
Nathaniel Gilbert's preaching and Coke's 1786 landing launched Methodist missions to enslaved people across the British Caribbean.
Black Loyalist Methodists from Nova Scotia founded congregations in Freetown; WMMS missionaries followed in 1811.
Coke's party established missions at Jaffna, Galle, Matara and Colombo, with Tamil and Sinhala schools.
Barnabas Shaw in Namaqualand and William Shaw's chain of stations in the Eastern Cape; Methodism became one of South Africa's largest churches.

American Methodists at Fuzhou (1847) and British Wesleyans in Guangdong (1851) and Hubei.
Henry Appenzeller and Mary Scranton founded Paichai and Ewha schools in Seoul; the Korean Methodist Church became autonomous in 1930.

journeys.title: John and Charles Wesley's voyage to Georgia (1735–1736)
journeys.people: John and Charles Wesley, Benjamin Ingham and Charles Delamotte, with Moravian emigrants
journeys.text: On the Simmonds the Wesleys sailed with 26 Moravians led by David Nitschmann; their calm singing during an Atlantic storm convinced John Wesley that he lacked their faith. His ministry in Savannah ended in controversy and he returned to England in 1737.

journeys.title: Whitefield's American preaching tour (1739–1740)
journeys.people: George Whitefield
journeys.text: Whitefield's tour from the middle colonies to Georgia and, in autumn 1740, through New England, where he preached in Jonathan Edwards's pulpit, drew crowds of thousands and turned local revivals into the intercolonial Great Awakening. Benjamin Franklin printed his sermons and journals.

journeys.title: Thomas Coke's storm-driven voyage to the West Indies (1786–1787)
journeys.people: Thomas Coke with William Warrener, William Hammet and John Clarke
journeys.text: Bound for Nova Scotia, Coke's ship was blown south and landed at Antigua on Christmas Day 1786. He left Warrener in Antigua, Clarke in St Vincent and Hammet in St Kitts, then sailed on to the American Methodist conference.

journeys.title: Coke's last voyage and the Ceylon mission (1813–1814)
journeys.people: Thomas Coke, James Lynch, William Ault, George Erskine, William Harvard, Thomas Squance and Benjamin Clough
journeys.text: The party sailed at the end of December 1813; Coke was found dead in his cabin on 3 May 1814 and buried at sea. The others reached Bombay and went on to Ceylon, landing at Galle in June 1814 to begin Methodist work in Asia.

journeys.title: Thomas Birch Freeman's journeys to Kumasi and Abeokuta (1838–1842)
journeys.people: Thomas Birch Freeman
journeys.text: Freeman walked to the Asante capital in 1839, where the Asantehene received him, then in 1842 visited Badagry and Abeokuta at the invitation of returning Sierra Leonean Yoruba Christians, opening the Methodist Nigeria mission.

relations.text: William Booth was a Methodist New Connexion minister, and Wesleyan teaching on entire sanctification was the root of the nineteenth-century Holiness movement.
Through the Holiness movement, Methodist perfectionism and camp-meeting revivalism fed directly into early Pentecostalism.
American Methodists, with Presbyterians, founded Korean Protestantism from 1885, and Korean Methodists took part in the 1907 revival.
Evangelical Anglicans who founded the CMS were products of the same Evangelical Revival, and the two movements often worked side by side.

agreements.text: Both stressed assurance, small-group discipline, hymnody and early mission to the enslaved.
Methodists such as John R. Mott were leading figures at Edinburgh 1910 and in the International Missionary Council and World Council of Churches.

disagreements.text: Wesley left the Fetter Lane Society in 1740 over Moravian 'stillness' and criticised what he saw as antinomianism in Zinzendorf.
Wesleyan Arminianism (Christ died for all) clashed with the Calvinism of Particular Baptists and of Whitefield's Calvinistic Methodists, though Carey's Fullerism narrowed the practical gap.

deviations: Wesley intended Methodism as a renewal society within the Church of England, but his ordinations for America (1784) and the Plan of Pacification (1795) made it a separate church.
American Methodism abandoned Wesley's rules against slaveholding in order to grow in the South, and the church split in 1844.
Later Methodism, especially in the West, largely abandoned the class meeting and the emphasis on entire sanctification that defined early Methodism.

missions.name: Baptist Missionary Society (William Carey, 1792)
missions.statusNote: Renamed BMS World Mission in 2000 and based at Didcot, the society still sends and supports workers in Asia, Africa, Latin America and Europe. The churches it founded are autonomous: Baptist unions and conventions in Bengal, Orissa, Mizoram, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Jamaica, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Angola, and BMS-related north Indian congregations within the Church of North India.
missions.summary: The first of the British voluntary missionary societies, founded at Kettering on 2 October 1792 by Particular Baptist ministers after William Carey's Enquiry argued that Christians were obliged to 'use means' to evangelise the world. Carey's voyage to Bengal in 1793 and the Serampore mission of Carey, Joshua and Hannah Marshman and William Ward made Bible translation, printing, education and social reform hallmarks of the modern missionary movement. The society went on to shape Baptist Christianity in Jamaica, Cameroon, Congo and China, and became a model for the voluntary society everywhere.
missions.story:
Late eighteenth-century English Particular Baptists were emerging from a 'hyper-Calvinism' that discouraged offering the gospel to the unconverted. Andrew Fuller's The Gospel Worthy of All Acceptation (1785) argued that all hearers had a duty to believe, and a network of Northamptonshire ministers (Fuller, John Ryland, John Sutcliff) began a 'Prayer Call' in 1784 for the spread of the gospel, influenced by Jonathan Edwards's Humble Attempt. William Carey, a shoemaker turned pastor at Moulton and Leicester who had taught himself languages and devoured Cook's Voyages, published An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens in May 1792, surveying the world's population by religion and citing the Moravians, the Danish mission, Eliot and Brainerd. His sermon at Nottingham on 31 May 1792, remembered as 'Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God', led to the founding meeting in the house of the widow Beeby Wallis at Kettering on 2 October 1792, where twelve ministers and a student pledged £13 2s 6d to the 'Particular Baptist Society for Propagating the Gospel among the Heathen'. Fuller was secretary until his death in 1815.

Carey and John Thomas, a surgeon who had already evangelised in Bengal, were to go to India. Without an East India Company licence they were put off their first ship at the Isle of Wight; they sailed instead on the Danish Kron Princessa Maria from Dover on 13 June 1793 with Carey's reluctant wife Dorothy, their children and her sister, and landed at Calcutta in November 1793. Poor and unlicensed, Carey managed an indigo factory at Mudnabati in Malda district (1794–99), learned Bengali and Sanskrit, and translated the New Testament. Dorothy's mental health collapsed after the death of their son Peter, one of the mission's hidden costs.

In 1799 Joshua and Hannah Marshman and William Ward, a printer, arrived and, barred by the Company, settled under Danish protection at Serampore, where Carey joined them on 10 January 1800. The 'Serampore Trio' ran a community household, schools and a great press. Krishna Pal, a carpenter, became the first Bengali convert baptised, on 28 December 1800, and the Bengali New Testament appeared in 1801. Carey taught Bengali, Sanskrit and Marathi at the Company's Fort William College from 1801. The Serampore Form of Agreement (1805) set out the mission's principles. By 1834 the Serampore press had produced complete Bibles or portions in about 44 languages and dialects, as well as grammars, dictionaries and editions of Sanskrit classics such as the Ramayana; much of the work was revised by others, and a fire in 1812 destroyed type and manuscripts. Serampore College opened in 1818 and received a Danish royal charter to grant degrees in 1827. Carey also campaigned against sati and infanticide and translated the 1829 regulation abolishing sati into Bengali.

Relations between Serampore's independent-minded veterans and a new generation of missionaries and committee members after Fuller's death led to a painful separation between 1827 and 1837. Meanwhile the society spread: Burma (1807), Ceylon (1812), Java (1813), Orissa through the General Baptist Missionary Society (1816, merged with the BMS in 1891), and Jamaica (1814). In Jamaica the BMS built on Black Baptist churches founded by George Liele, a formerly enslaved preacher from Georgia, from 1783. When the enslaved Baptist deacon Samuel Sharpe led the 'Baptist War' rising of 1831–32, planters burned chapels and blamed missionaries; William Knibb's campaign in Britain in 1832 strengthened the case for emancipation, enacted in 1833–34 with full freedom in 1838. Baptist missionaries such as James Phillippo then founded 'free villages' for the formerly enslaved.

Jamaican and British Baptists together began a West African mission at Fernando Po in 1841, moving to Cameroon, where Joseph Merrick (a Jamaican) and Alfred Saker translated Scripture into Duala and Saker founded Victoria (Limbe) in 1858. In 1878 the BMS entered the Congo: Thomas Comber and George Grenfell reached São Salvador (Mbanza Kongo) in 1879 and Stanley Pool in 1881, and Grenfell explored the river system in the steamer Peace from 1884. In China, Timothy Richard (from 1870) organised famine relief in Shanxi in 1876–79 and became an influential advocate of reform; the society lost missionaries in the Boxer killings in Shanxi in 1900.

In the twentieth century BMS missions worked toward church autonomy, joined ecumenical schemes (North Indian Baptists joined the Church of North India in 1970, while other Baptist unions remained separate), and supported medical work in Congo and Nepal (through the United Mission to Nepal) and new work in Brazil (1953) and Angola. The society also had to reckon with its record in the Congo Free State, where its missionaries were slow to denounce King Leopold's regime. Renamed BMS World Mission in 2000, it remains active, while Carey is commemorated in India as a pioneer of Bengali prose, printing and education.
beliefs: Evangelical Calvinism as reformulated by Andrew Fuller: God is sovereign in salvation, yet the gospel is to be offered freely to all and all have a duty to believe.
The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19–20) is binding on the church in every age, not only on the apostles, as Carey's Enquiry argued.
Believers' baptism by immersion and gathered congregations of professing believers.
Christians are obliged to 'use means' (voluntary societies, money, training and translation) to spread the gospel.
A postmillennial hope that the world would be evangelised before Christ's return, encouraging long-range planning and optimism.
Every people should have the Scriptures in their own language, which made translation the core missionary task.
strategies: The voluntary society: subscribers, a committee and a secretary independent of any church hierarchy, a model copied by the LMS, CMS and American Board.
Bible translation and printing on an industrial scale at the Serampore Mission Press.
Education at every level, from vernacular schools to Serampore College (1818), with degree-granting powers from 1827.

The Serampore Form of Agreement (1805): study the people's beliefs and ways of thinking, avoid needless offence, preach Christ crucified, train Indian preachers and live frugally with property held in common.
Self-support through secular work: Carey's indigo management, Marshman's boarding schools and Carey's salary from Fort William College funded the mission.
Social reform campaigns, including against sati, infanticide and slavery, and advocacy for emancipated people in Jamaica.
Exploration and river steamers to open interior Africa, as in Grenfell's Congo work.
groupsReached: Bengali Hindus and Muslims in Bengal, including Krishna Pal and early converts from artisan and lower castes.
Oriya-speaking people in Orissa and, later, Mizo and Bengali-speaking groups in north-east India and Bangladesh.
Enslaved and free Africans and Afro-Jamaicans in Jamaica and the Bahamas.
Duala and Bakweri peoples of coastal Cameroon.
Kongo, Bobangi and other peoples of the lower and middle Congo River.
Rural Chinese in Shandong and Shanxi, and Sinhala and Tamil communities in Ceylon.
challenges: East India Company hostility to missionaries until the Charter Act of 1813, which forced the Serampore mission to work from Danish territory.
Disease and mortality: in Congo dozens of BMS missionaries died in the first decades, including Thomas Comber and his wife.
Low numbers of converts in Bengal; social ostracism of converts who broke caste.
Internal conflict: the Serampore schism (1827–37) over control of property and policy.
Planter opposition and violence in Jamaica, culminating in chapel-burning after the 1831–32 rising.
Financial strain, including the 1812 Serampore fire, which destroyed type, paper and manuscripts.
harms: William Ward's View of the History, Literature and Religion of the Hindoos (1811) portrayed Hinduism in contemptuous terms that shaped British prejudice for decades.
Converts were required to break caste completely, often at the cost of family and livelihood, leaving them dependent on the mission.
Carey's family paid a heavy price: Dorothy Carey was taken to India against her early wishes and suffered severe mental illness.

In the Congo Free State, BMS leaders including Grenfell initially cooperated with King Leopold's regime and were slow to protest its atrocities, which were exposed chiefly by others such as the Harrises and E. D. Morel.
Mission paternalism delayed the transfer of authority to Indian and African leaders well into the twentieth century.
developments: Created the model of the voluntary missionary society that launched the 'Great Century' of Protestant missions.
Pioneered Bengali prose, printing and lexicography; Carey's grammars and dictionaries were standard works.
Serampore College (1818), whose 1827 charter made it one of the earliest degree-granting institutions in Asia.
Contributed to the abolition of sati in 1829 and to anti-slavery agitation that hastened emancipation in the British Caribbean.
Founded strong Baptist churches in Jamaica, Cameroon, Congo, Orissa, Mizoram and Bangladesh that are now self-governing.
Inspired the conversion of Adoniram and Ann Judson to Baptist views and thereby the American Baptist foreign mission.
missions.outcome: The BMS turned a small Northamptonshire ministers' circle into the prototype of modern Protestant missions. Its translation and educational work at Serampore had a lasting cultural impact in Bengal; its churches in Jamaica, Cameroon, Congo and India are autonomous; and the society continues as BMS World Mission.
