journeys.people: William and Dorothy Carey, their children, Catherine Plackett and John Thomas

stops.name: Ryde, Isle of Wight (first attempt abandoned)

journeys.text: Turned off the Earl of Oxford at the Isle of Wight for lack of a Company licence, Carey sailed from Dover on the Danish Kron Princessa Maria on 13 June 1793 with his whole family, reaching Calcutta in November after five months at sea. After a hungry winter on a grant of land in the Sundarbans he managed an indigo works at Mudnabati, and in January 1800 joined Marshman and Ward at Danish Serampore.

journeys.title: William Knibb between Jamaica and Britain (1824–1834)
journeys.people: William Knibb
journeys.text: Knibb arrived in Jamaica in 1825, ministered at Falmouth, was arrested after the 1831–32 rising, and in 1832 toured Britain describing the persecution of Baptist slaves, a campaign that helped secure the Emancipation Act of 1833.

journeys.title: The Jamaican-British Baptist mission to Fernando Po and Cameroon (1843–1858)
journeys.people: Alfred Saker, Joseph Merrick, John Clarke and Jamaican Baptist settlers
journeys.text: A party of Jamaican Baptists sailed to Fernando Po in 1843–44 to evangelise West Africa. When Spain expelled Protestant missionaries from the island, Saker led the settlers to the mainland, founding Victoria in 1858; he had already established the mission at Douala, where he printed the Duala Bible.

journeys.title: Comber and Grenfell open the Congo mission (1878–1896)
journeys.people: Thomas Comber and George Grenfell
journeys.text: Funded by the Leeds merchant Robert Arthington, the pioneers established São Salvador in 1879, reached Stanley Pool by 1881 and from 1884 used the steamer Peace to explore and plant stations along the middle Congo, reaching the region of Stanley Falls by the 1890s.

relations.text: News of Carey's mission, especially his letters from Bengal, inspired the London ministers who founded the Missionary Society (LMS) in 1795.

Adoniram and Ann Judson became Baptists on the way to India and were baptised at Calcutta in 1812 by Serampore missionaries; Luther Rice's appeal led American Baptists to form their own mission society.
The British and Foreign Bible Society (1804) funded much of Serampore's translation and printing.
The example of the BMS and LMS encouraged Evangelical Anglicans to form a society within their own church in 1799.

agreements.text: Both were evangelical voluntary societies committed to translation, preaching and education, and cooperated in India and in anti-slavery campaigns.
Serampore consciously continued the Tranquebar model of translation, printing, schools and Danish protection.

disagreements.text: Carey and Serampore prioritised vernacular languages and Sanskrit learning, while Alexander Duff (from 1830) championed English-medium higher education as the way to reach Bengal's elite.
As Calvinists, Particular Baptists rejected Wesleyan Arminianism and perfectionism, though both were evangelical and cooperated in practice.

deviations: The Serampore missionaries' independence led to an open breach with the society they had served (1827–37), contrary to the founders' vision of a single united mission.
Some BMS leaders in Congo accommodated themselves to the Free State regime in a way at odds with the society's anti-slavery heritage.
Timothy Richard's sympathetic approach to Buddhism and Chinese religion drew criticism from evangelicals that he had moved beyond the society's founding theology.

missions.name: London Missionary Society (1795: Tahiti, Madagascar, Moffat, Livingstone)

origin.name: London (Spa Fields and the Castle and Falcon, Aldersgate)

missions.statusNote: In 1966 the LMS merged with the Commonwealth Missionary Society to form the Congregational Council for World Mission, and in 1977 it was restructured as the Council for World Mission (CWM), a partnership of about 30 member churches, most of them former LMS fields in the Pacific, Africa, India and East Asia, which share resources and decision-making as equals.
missions.summary: Founded in 1795 as 'the Missionary Society' by evangelical Congregationalists, Anglicans, Presbyterians and Methodists, the LMS aimed to send 'not Presbyterianism, Independency, Episcopacy, or any other form of church government', but 'the glorious Gospel of the blessed God'. Its ship Duff carried thirty missionaries to Tahiti in 1796–97, beginning Protestant Christianity in Polynesia; it went on to plant churches in South Africa, Madagascar, India, China, Siberia, Guyana and New Guinea, through figures such as John Williams, Robert Moffat, David Livingstone, Robert Morrison and James Chalmers, and through hundreds of Pacific Islander and African evangelists.
missions.story:
Stirred by Carey's letters from Bengal and by the evangelical revival, ministers including David Bogue of Gosport, the Anglican Thomas Haweis and John Eyre met from 1794 and founded the Missionary Society in London on 22 September 1795. Its 'Fundamental Principle' (1796) declared that the society would send the gospel without any particular form of church order, leaving converts to choose their own; in practice, as Anglicans and Presbyterians formed their own societies, the LMS became chiefly Congregationalist. It was renamed the London Missionary Society in 1818.

The first venture was dramatic. The society bought the ship Duff and, under Captain James Wilson, sent thirty missionaries, only four of them ordained (the rest artisans such as carpenters, weavers, a bricklayer and a surgeon), some accompanied by wives and children. Leaving the Thames on 10 August 1796 and Portsmouth in September, the Duff called at Rio de Janeiro, rounded the Cape of Good Hope and crossed the Southern Ocean to Tahiti, anchoring in Matavai Bay on 5 March 1797. Eighteen missionaries landed there; others were left on Tongatapu and on Tahuata in the Marquesas before the ship returned via Canton. The Tonga and Marquesas missions failed within a few years, and most of the Tahiti party fled to New South Wales in 1798. A remnant led by Henry Nott persisted, and in 1812 the chief Pomare II asked for baptism; after his victory at Fei Pi in 1815 Tahiti rapidly became Christian, and the missionaries helped draft the Pomare Code of 1819. Nott completed the Tahitian Bible in 1835.

From Tahiti and the Society Islands, John Williams turned the mission outward. With Raiatean and Tahitian teachers such as Papeiha, who landed on Aitutaki in 1821 and Rarotonga in 1823, he spread Christianity to the Cook Islands, sailed his own ship, the Messenger of Peace, to Samoa in 1830, and was killed on landing at Dillon's Bay on Erromango in the New Hebrides on 20 November 1839. Pacific Islander teachers, many of whom also died, carried the faith on to Niue, Tuvalu, the Loyalty Islands and, from 1871, to Papua, where W. G. Lawes settled at Port Moresby in 1874 and James Chalmers was killed on Goaribari Island in 1901.

In South Africa the Dutch physician Johannes van der Kemp began work among the Khoikhoi in 1799 and founded Bethelsdorp in 1803; his successor as superintendent, John Philip, published Researches in South Africa (1828), which helped secure Ordinance 50 (1828) granting the Khoikhoi legal rights, and made him hated by settlers. Robert and Mary Moffat founded Kuruman in 1824 among the Tlhaping (Tswana), where Moffat printed the complete Setswana Bible in 1857. Their daughter Mary married David Livingstone, who arrived in 1841 and moved north to Mabotsa and Kolobeng; with few converts, he turned to exploration, crossing the Kalahari to Lake Ngami (1849), reaching the Zambezi (1851), crossing Africa from Luanda to Quelimane (1853–56) and publicising the East African slave trade. He resigned from the LMS in 1857, but his call for 'Christianity and commerce' shaped Victorian mission and empire for decades. Further north the LMS entered Matabeleland at Inyati (1859) and Lake Tanganyika (1877).

In Madagascar the Welsh missionaries David Jones and Thomas Bevan arrived in 1818; under King Radama I the mission opened schools and printed the Malagasy Bible (1835) in the Latin script. Queen Ranavalona I then banned Christianity (1835), and during a quarter-century of persecution many Christians were killed, among them Rasalama (1837), while the church grew underground. Ranavalona II was baptised in 1869 and ordered the burning of the royal sampy (talismans), making Protestant Christianity the religion of the Merina state, before French conquest in 1895–96. In Asia, Robert Morrison reached Canton in 1807 as the first Protestant missionary to China, completing a Chinese Bible with William Milne by 1823; the Anglo-Chinese College at Malacca, James Legge's translations of the Chinese Classics and Griffith John's work in Hankow followed. In South India Ringeltaube (from 1806) began the Travancore mission, whose churches grew among Nadars and Dalits; in Siberia Edward Stallybrass and William Swan translated the Bible into Mongolian among the Buryats (1817–40); and in Demerara (Guyana) the missionary John Smith died in prison in 1824 after being blamed for the 1823 slave rising.

The twentieth century brought devolution. LMS churches in South India joined the Church of South India in 1947, Chinese congregations entered the Church of Christ in China (1927) and later the post-1949 Three-Self structures, the Malagasy churches formed the FJKM in 1968, and Pacific churches became the Congregational Christian Church of Samoa, Ekalesia Kelisiano Tuvalu and others. In 1977 the LMS turned itself into the Council for World Mission, in which the former 'mission fields' are equal partners with the British churches.
beliefs: Evangelical, broadly Calvinist Protestantism centred on the atoning death of Christ, the need for conversion and the authority of Scripture.
The 'Fundamental Principle' (1796): mission should spread the gospel, not a denominational form of church government, leaving converts to decide their church order.
Congregational polity in practice: self-governing local churches of professing believers.
A belief, shared by most missionaries, that Christianity, literacy, commerce and 'civilisation' went together, articulated most famously by Livingstone.
Anti-slavery conviction: many LMS missionaries opposed the slave trade and advocated for the rights of Khoikhoi, enslaved Africans and Pacific Islanders.
Postmillennial optimism that the gospel would steadily spread to all nations.
strategies: Sending artisan missionaries to model 'civilised' Christian life, as on the Duff in 1796.
Bible translation and printing: Tahitian, Rarotongan, Samoan, Setswana, Malagasy, Chinese, Mongolian and many other languages.
Use of Pacific Islander and African teachers and evangelists as the main agents of expansion, with European missionaries as supervisors.
Mission ships (the Duff, Camden, Messenger of Peace and a series of John Williams ships) linking scattered island stations.
Education, from village schools to colleges such as the Anglo-Chinese College (Malacca, 1818), Malua Theological College in Samoa (1844) and Tiger Kloof in South Africa (1904).
Political advocacy on behalf of indigenous peoples, as in John Philip's campaign at the Cape.
Medical missions, notably in China and India.
groupsReached: Tahitians and Society Islanders, Cook Islanders, Samoans, Niueans, Tuvaluans, Loyalty Islanders and peoples of Papua.
Khoikhoi, Griqua, Tswana, Ndebele and Xhosa peoples of Southern Africa.
Merina and other peoples of Madagascar.
Cantonese and other Chinese communities in Southeast Asia and China.
Nadars and Dalit communities (Pulayas, Parayas) of South Travancore in India, and Telugu and Kannada speakers in Andhra and Karnataka.
Buryat Mongols in Siberia, Mongols in Inner Mongolia, and enslaved Africans in Demerara and Berbice (Guyana).
challenges: Early failures: the Duff missionaries largely abandoned Tahiti in 1798, and the Tonga and Marquesas missions collapsed.
Violence: missionaries and Islander teachers were killed in the New Hebrides and Papua, and Christians were persecuted in Madagascar (1835–61).
Disease and isolation, especially in central Africa and the Pacific.
Settler and planter hostility in the Cape Colony and Demerara toward missionary advocacy for indigenous and enslaved people.
Competition with Catholic, Anglican and other missions, as with French Catholic missions in Tahiti and Anglican missions in Madagascar.
Political upheaval in China (Taiping war, Boxer rising, the 1949 revolution), which ended LMS work there.
harms: Missionary partisanship in Pacific politics: support for Pomare II's war of 1815 and the Pomare Code of 1819, which imposed missionary moral law with penalties.
Destruction of religious objects and sacred sites in Tahiti, Rarotonga and Madagascar (the burning of the sampy in 1869), and suppression of dance, tattooing and other customs.

In 1888 the LMS missionary Charles Helm witnessed and interpreted the Rudd Concession, misleading Lobengula about its terms, and John Smith Moffat (a former LMS missionary) negotiated the Moffat Treaty, both preparing for Rhodes's seizure of Matabeleland.
The Madagascar mission's identification with the Merina monarchy made Protestantism a state religion that subject peoples experienced as Merina domination.
George Pritchard's role as both missionary and British consul in Tahiti entangled the mission in the Anglo-French crisis of 1843–44 and the expulsion of Catholic priests in 1836.
Paternalism toward Islander teachers, who bore the greatest risks but received little recognition or authority until late in the mission's history.
developments: Founded the Protestant churches of Polynesia, which remain central to national life in Samoa, Tuvalu, the Cook Islands, Niue and French Polynesia.
Translations of the Bible into Tahitian, Setswana, Malagasy, Chinese, Mongolian and many Pacific languages, with grammars and dictionaries.
Advocacy for indigenous rights, from Ordinance 50 at the Cape (1828) to campaigns against slavery and blackbirding.
Morrison's and Legge's sinology, which shaped Western understanding of Chinese language and classics.
Schools and colleges that educated generations of African, Malagasy, Indian and Pacific leaders.
The Council for World Mission (1977), a pioneering model of mission partnership among equals.
missions.outcome: The LMS was one of the most influential Protestant missions of the nineteenth century, creating whole national churches in the South Pacific and Madagascar and significant ones in South Africa, India and China. Having become largely Congregationalist despite its non-denominational founding principle, it reconstituted itself in 1977 as the Council for World Mission, owned jointly by the churches it had helped to found.

Raiatean teachers Papeiha and Vahapata, then Williams and Aaron Buzacott; the Cook Islands Christian Church.
Williams and Tahitian teachers landed at Sapapali'i; Malua College (1844) trained Samoan pastors who served across the Pacific.
Bethelsdorp, Philip's advocacy, Moffat's Kuruman and Livingstone's stations at Mabotsa and Kolobeng.
Schools and translation under Radama I, persecution under Ranavalona I, and the conversion of the Merina monarchy in 1869.
Morrison at Canton and Macau, then Hong Kong, Shanghai, Hankow and Beijing; churches joined the Church of Christ in China (1927).
William Milne's press and the Anglo-Chinese College (1818) served the Chinese diaspora before China opened.
Missions in Travancore (Nagercoil, Neyyoor), Bellary, Cuddapah, Vizagapatam and Bengal; South Indian churches joined the CSI in 1947.
John Wray and John Smith among enslaved Africans; Smith's death in prison (1824) fed British abolitionism.
Stallybrass and Swan translated the Bible into literary Mongolian until Nicholas I closed the mission in 1840.
Inyati mission among the Ndebele; LMS missionaries were drawn into the concessions that preceded colonisation.
Loyalty Islander and Samoan teachers, Lawes at Port Moresby (1874) and Chalmers along the coast; today the United Church in Papua New Guinea.
Central African mission at Ujiji and later Mbereshi and Kawimbe, with heavy losses to disease.
Samoan and other Islander pastors founded churches that became national churches.

journeys.title: The voyage of the Duff to Tahiti, Tonga and the Marquesas (1796–1798)
journeys.people: Captain James Wilson and thirty LMS missionaries, including Henry Nott and John Jefferson
journeys.text: The Duff left the Thames on 10 August 1796 and, after calling at Rio de Janeiro, went east round the Cape of Good Hope and south of Australia to reach Matavai Bay on 5 March 1797, where eighteen missionaries landed. Ten were left on Tongatapu and two on Tahuata; the ship returned to Tahiti and then sailed home by way of Canton, reaching England in July 1798.

journeys.title: John Williams's Pacific voyages (1817–1839)
journeys.people: John Williams, Mary Williams and Islander teachers including Papeiha
journeys.text: Based at Raiatea, Williams placed Islander teachers on Aitutaki and Rarotonga, built the Messenger of Peace on Rarotonga in 1827, and landed Tahitian teachers in Samoa in 1830. Returning to the Pacific after a celebrated tour of Britain, he was clubbed to death with James Harris on Erromango on 20 November 1839.

journeys.title: Robert Morrison's voyage to China via New York (1807)
journeys.people: Robert Morrison
journeys.text: Refused passage by the East India Company, Morrison sailed in January 1807 to New York and then on the American ship Trident to Macau and Canton, arriving in September 1807, where he lived precariously as an American-protected foreigner while learning Chinese.

journeys.title: Livingstone's early journeys from Kuruman to the Zambezi (1841–1851)
journeys.people: David Livingstone, with William Cotton Oswell and Mary Livingstone
journeys.text: From Moffat's Kuruman, Livingstone moved north to Mabotsa, where a lion mauled him, and to Kolobeng among the Kwena of Sechele, his only baptised convert. With Oswell he crossed the Kalahari to Lake Ngami in 1849 and reached the upper Zambezi in 1851.

journeys.title: Livingstone's crossing of Africa from Luanda to Quelimane (1853–1856)
journeys.people: David Livingstone with Kololo companions
journeys.text: Seeking a healthy route into the interior for missions and 'legitimate commerce', Livingstone travelled with Kololo companions from Linyanti to the Atlantic at Luanda (May 1854), returned, and followed the Zambezi to the Indian Ocean, becoming the first European known to have seen Victoria Falls (November 1855). His Missionary Travels (1857) made him a national hero.

journeys.title: Livingstone's last journey (1866–1873, after leaving the LMS)
journeys.people: David Livingstone with Susi, Chuma, Jacob Wainwright and others
journeys.text: Searching for the Nile's sources, Livingstone witnessed the massacre of hundreds of Manyema people at the Nyangwe market by slave-traders' gunmen (July 1871), met H. M. Stanley at Ujiji, and died at Chitambo's village on 1 May 1873. Susi and Chuma carried his body some 1,500 km to the coast, and his burial in Westminster Abbey (1874) spurred new Scottish and Anglican missions to central Africa.

journeys.title: Jones and Bevan to Madagascar (1818–1820)
journeys.people: David Jones and Thomas Bevan
journeys.text: The two Welsh missionaries landed at Tamatave in 1818; fever killed Bevan and both families and nearly killed Jones, who recovered in Mauritius and in 1820 was welcomed by Radama I at Antananarivo, opening the first schools.

relations.text: The LMS's reliance on Tahitian, Rarotongan, Samoan and Loyalty Islander teachers created the Pacific Islander missionary movement.
Livingstone's death in 1873 prompted the Free Church of Scotland's Livingstonia (1875) and the Church of Scotland's Blantyre mission (1876).
The LMS and the American Board divided Pacific fields by comity and cooperated in Micronesia, Hawaii and China.
LMS leaders were active at Edinburgh 1910 and in the International Missionary Council, and the society's transformation into the Council for World Mission (1977) embodied ecumenical partnership.

agreements.text: Shared evangelical Calvinism, the voluntary-society model and priority on translation and education.
Many LMS missionaries (Moffat, Livingstone, Philip, Chalmers) were Scots, and the two shared Reformed theology and an emphasis on education.

disagreements.text: Anglican evangelicals withdrew to found the CMS in 1799 because the LMS was not church-based; later the two clashed over comity in Madagascar, where CMS missionaries worked from 1864 until withdrawing in 1874.

When Wesleyan missionaries entered Samoa in 1835, the LMS objected that the islands were its field; the British Wesleyans agreed to withdraw, but Samoan Methodists continued and Tongan Methodists later resumed the work, leaving lasting rivalry.

deviations: Founded as a non-denominational society, the LMS became in practice a Congregationalist body, contrary to its Fundamental Principle.
The Fundamental Principle promised converts freedom to choose their church order, but missionaries often imposed Congregational structures and English moral codes.
Missionaries such as Pritchard in Tahiti and Helm in Matabeleland took political roles that compromised the society's claim to be above politics.

missions.name: Church Missionary Society (1799: Venn's three-self principle, Crowther, East Africa)

origin.name: Castle and Falcon inn, Aldersgate Street, London

missions.statusNote: Renamed the Church Mission Society in 1995 and recognised as an Acknowledged Community of the Church of England in 2008, CMS continues to send and support mission workers and trains pioneer ministers. Its former fields are self-governing Anglican provinces, including the Church of Nigeria, the Church of Uganda and the Anglican Church of Kenya, which together make up a large share of the Anglican Communion's active membership and have become leading voices in it.
missions.summary: The evangelical Anglican mission society founded in London on 12 April 1799 by members of the Eclectic Society and the Clapham circle. Beginning with German Lutheran missionaries in Sierra Leone, it became the largest British missionary society of the nineteenth century, working in West and East Africa, India, New Zealand, Canada, China, Japan and the Middle East. Under Henry Venn it articulated the 'three-self' goal of self-supporting, self-governing and self-extending churches and consecrated Samuel Ajayi Crowther as the first African Anglican bishop (1864), though a later generation of missionaries undermined him. CMS-founded churches in Nigeria, Uganda and Kenya are now among the largest in the Anglican Communion.
missions.story:
Evangelical Anglicans of the Eclectic Society, among them John Venn of Clapham, Charles Simeon, John Newton, Henry Thornton and William Wilberforce, wanted a mission society that, unlike the non-denominational London Missionary Society, was faithful to the Church of England, but which, unlike the older SPG, was run by evangelicals. On 12 April 1799 they founded the Society for Missions to Africa and the East at the Castle and Falcon inn in Aldersgate Street; it took the name Church Missionary Society in 1812. Thomas Scott was its first secretary and Josiah Pratt its organiser. Because no English clergy volunteered at first, its first missionaries were German Lutherans trained at Johann Jänicke's Berlin seminary, Melchior Renner and Peter Hartwig, who sailed for Sierra Leone in 1804.

Sierra Leone became the society's first great field. After Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807, Royal Navy patrols landed tens of thousands of 'recaptives' liberated from slave ships at Freetown, and CMS missionaries such as W. A. B. Johnson at Regent (1816–23) gathered them into Christian villages. Fourah Bay Institution (1827), later affiliated to Durham University (1876), produced an educated West African clergy. Its first student was Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a Yoruba boy enslaved in 1821, freed by the Royal Navy in 1822 and baptised in 1825. Crowther joined the Niger Expedition of 1841, was ordained in London in 1843, translated the Bible into Yoruba, went to Abeokuta with Henry Townsend in 1846, and from 1857 led an all-African Niger Mission. Meanwhile CMS also entered New Zealand, where Samuel Marsden preached the first sermon on Christmas Day 1814 at Oihi in the Bay of Islands; Henry Williams later translated the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) into Māori, a translation whose differences from the English text remain at the centre of debate about Māori sovereignty.

Henry Venn, honorary secretary from 1841 to 1872, gave the society its theory of mission. In papers of 1851, 1855 and 1861 he argued that missions should aim at the 'euthanasia of a mission': the creation of native churches that were self-supporting, self-governing and self-extending, under native pastors and eventually native bishops, after which the missionaries would move on. In 1864, at Venn's urging, Crowther was consecrated in Canterbury Cathedral as bishop of 'the countries of Western Africa beyond the limits of the Queen's dominions'. In India CMS worked from Agra (where Abdul Masih, a convert of Henry Martyn, served from 1813), in Tirunelveli (where Rhenius and others built a mass movement among Nadars), in Travancore (a 'Mission of Help' to the Syrian Christians from 1816, which ended in a split in 1836 and ultimately in the Mar Thoma reform movement), and in the Punjab and on the North-West Frontier from 1852. Thomas Valpy French founded St John's College, Agra (1850), and became first bishop of Lahore (1877).

In East Africa the German CMS missionaries Johann Ludwig Krapf (who arrived at Mombasa in 1844, after earlier work in Ethiopia, and lost his wife and baby within weeks) and Johannes Rebmann settled at Rabai; Rebmann was the first European to report Kilimanjaro (1848) and Krapf Mount Kenya (1849). Frere Town (1875) near Mombasa received freed slaves. After H. M. Stanley's 1875 appeal from the court of Kabaka Mutesa I of Buganda, a CMS party reached the kingdom in 1877, followed in 1878 by the engineer Alexander Mackay. Under Kabaka Mwanga Christian converts were persecuted: Bishop James Hannington was killed in Busoga in October 1885, and in 1885–87 dozens of Anglican and Catholic pages and officials were executed, the Uganda Martyrs. After civil wars between Protestant, Catholic and Muslim factions (1888–92), CMS supporters lobbied the British government to retain Uganda, which became a protectorate in 1894; the Anglican chiefs led by Apolo Kagwa dominated the kingdom, and Baganda evangelists such as Apolo Kivebulaya carried Christianity to Toro and the Congo.

The 1880s brought a crisis in the Niger Mission. Young, Keswick-influenced English missionaries, among them G. W. Brooke and J. A. Robinson, accused Crowther's African clergy of laxity and took control of the mission's finances in 1890; Crowther died in 1891 and was succeeded by a European bishop. The affair, which historians including J. F. Ade Ajayi, Andrew Walls and Jehu Hanciles treat as a turning point, discredited Venn's policy for a generation and contributed to the formation of African-led churches such as the United Native African Church (1891) and the Niger Delta Pastorate under James Johnson. In the same era CMS grew dramatically through university recruits inspired by the 'Cambridge Seven' and Keswick, entering Japan (1869), Persia (1869), China (Ningbo 1848, Fujian 1850, where eleven CMS and CEZMS missionaries and children were killed at Kucheng in 1895) and Canada's Rupert's Land, where it had worked since 1822 and ordained Henry Budd, the first Indigenous Anglican priest in North America, in 1850.

In the twentieth century CMS-related churches in Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda were transformed by the East African Revival (from 1929–35, among CMS missionaries such as Joe Church and Africans such as Simeon Nsibambi), while CMS clashed with Kikuyu leaders over female circumcision (1929–31) and later navigated Mau Mau. Under Max Warren (general secretary 1942–63) CMS became a thoughtful voice on mission after empire. The provinces it helped create became autonomous, among them Nigeria (1979), Uganda (1961) and Kenya (1970), and Nigerian, Ugandan and Kenyan Anglicans have since become numerically and theologically prominent in the Anglican Communion, notably in GAFCON. The society itself, renamed the Church Mission Society in 1995, now presents mission as a two-way relationship and sends mission partners from and to every continent.
beliefs: Evangelical Anglicanism: the authority of Scripture, justification by faith, the necessity of conversion, the Book of Common Prayer and the Thirty-Nine Articles.
Loyalty to the episcopal order of the Church of England, with mission conducted by a voluntary society within the church rather than by the hierarchy.
Venn's 'three-self' principle: missions should create self-supporting, self-governing and self-extending native churches and then withdraw ('the euthanasia of a mission').
Opposition to the slave trade and slavery, inherited from the Clapham Sect, and a belief in 'legitimate commerce' and education as the alternative.
In the later nineteenth century, Keswick holiness spirituality and premillennial urgency shaped many recruits.
strategies: Settlements and schools for liberated Africans and freed slaves (Freetown villages, Frere Town).
Training indigenous clergy and teachers: Fourah Bay College (1827), CMS College Kottayam (1815), St John's College Agra (1850), Bishop Tucker College Mukono (1913).
Vernacular translation: Yoruba (Crowther), Igbo, Luganda, Swahili (Krapf), Māori, Malayalam (Benjamin Bailey) and other languages.
Appointing indigenous bishops and pastorates under Venn, beginning with Crowther (1864) and the Sierra Leone Native Pastorate (1861).
Medical missions such as Mengo Hospital in Kampala (1897, Albert Cook) and hospitals in Amritsar, Peshawar and Multan.
Political lobbying in Britain, as in the campaign to retain Uganda (1892) and in anti-slavery causes.
Women's missionary work through CMS women missionaries and allied societies such as the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society.
groupsReached: Liberated Africans (recaptives) of many origins in Sierra Leone, and Krio society.
Yoruba, Igbo, Ijaw and other peoples of southern Nigeria and the Niger Delta.
Baganda, Basoga, Banyoro, Batoro and other peoples of Uganda; Kikuyu, Luo and Mijikenda in Kenya; Rwandans, Burundians and Tanzanians.
Māori in New Zealand.
Nadars and Dalits in Tirunelveli, Syrian Christians and Dalits in Travancore, and urban and Punjabi communities in North India and Pakistan.
Cree and other First Nations in Rupert's Land and British Columbia; Chinese in Fujian and Zhejiang; Japanese, Persians, Egyptians and Palestinians.
challenges: A shortage of English clergy in the early decades, making the society dependent on German Lutheran missionaries.
Very high mortality in West Africa: dozens of CMS missionaries died in Sierra Leone in the society's first two decades.
Tension with bishops and high-church Anglicans over the society's evangelical independence.
Political violence: persecution in Buganda (1885–87), religious civil wars there (1888–92), the Kucheng massacre in China (1895).
Resistance from Hindu, Muslim and Buddhist communities and very slow growth among Muslims in North India, Persia and Egypt.
Racial tension between missionaries and African and Asian clergy, culminating in the Niger crisis of 1887–91.
harms: The humiliation of Bishop Crowther and his African clergy by young European missionaries (1887–91), and the appointment of white successors, set back African church leadership for half a century.
CMS lobbying helped secure British imperial rule over Uganda, and Anglican chiefs used the protectorate to entrench Protestant political dominance.
In New Zealand missionaries' land purchases and the ambiguous Māori translation of the Treaty of Waitangi contributed to Māori dispossession.
CMS-founded schools for First Nations children in Canada fed into the residential school system, now recognised as gravely harmful.
Missionary campaigns against female circumcision in Kenya (1929–31) were pursued with expulsions from church and school that alienated many Kikuyu.
The Travancore 'Mission of Help' to the Syrian Christians ended in mutual recrimination and schism in 1836.
developments: Venn's three-self formula, which (with Rufus Anderson's parallel theory) became the standard Protestant goal for mission churches worldwide.
The first African Anglican bishop (Crowther, 1864) and a Yoruba Bible and literature that shaped Yoruba written culture.
Large, self-governing Anglican churches in Nigeria, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda and South India.
Educational institutions such as Fourah Bay College, CMS College Kottayam, King's College Budo and Mengo Hospital.
Linguistic scholarship, including Krapf's Swahili dictionary and grammar.
The East African Revival, a lay renewal movement that spread across East Africa and beyond.
missions.outcome: CMS was the largest and one of the most influential British missionary societies, and its legacy is above all the Anglican churches of Nigeria, Uganda, Kenya and their neighbours, now among the most vigorous parts of the Anglican Communion. Venn's three-self vision, abandoned in the Niger crisis, was later vindicated by the churches it helped create, and the society continues as the Church Mission Society.

countries.text: Recaptive villages, Fourah Bay College and the Sierra Leone Native Pastorate (1861), the first self-governing CMS church.
Marsden's mission at Oihi and later Paihia and Waimate; Henry Williams's role in the Treaty of Waitangi; Māori Anglicanism.
Agra, Tirunelveli, Travancore, Bengal, the Punjab and Peshawar; CMS churches joined the Church of South India (1947), the Church of North India (1970) and the Church of Pakistan (1970).
Badagry and Abeokuta among the Yoruba, Crowther's Niger Mission from 1857, and the Church of Nigeria, now the largest Anglican province.
Krapf and Rebmann at Rabai, Frere Town, and later work among the Kikuyu and Luo; the Anglican Church of Kenya.
Mission at the Buganda court, the Uganda Martyrs, the protectorate and the rapid growth of the Church of Uganda.
Mission among Cree and other First Nations from Red River; Henry Budd ordained 1850; William Duncan's Metlakatla on the Pacific coast (1862).
Missions in Ningbo, Hangzhou, Fujian and Sichuan; the Kucheng massacre of 1895.
Work in Nagasaki, Osaka and Hokkaido, including among the Ainu (John Batchelor); part of the Nippon Sei Ko Kai.
Missions in Jerusalem and Nazareth (1851), Isfahan (1869) and Cairo (1882), with schools and hospitals but few converts from Islam.
Peshawar mission and hospitals at Peshawar, Bannu and Quetta (Theodore Pennell at Bannu).
The Ruanda Mission (CMS), with Gahini as the cradle of the East African Revival.
Mission stations in central Tanganyika (Mpwapwa) and later the Diocese of Central Tanganyika.

journeys.title: Crowther on the Niger Expedition (1841)
journeys.people: Samuel Ajayi Crowther and J. F. Schön with the British Niger Expedition
journeys.text: The government expedition, intended to found a model farm and suppress the slave trade, lost about forty of its roughly 150 Europeans to fever, but Crowther's journals persuaded CMS that Africans must evangelise Africa. He returned to lead the Niger Mission in 1857.

journeys.title: Marsden's first voyage to New Zealand (1814)
journeys.people: Samuel Marsden with Thomas Kendall, William Hall, John King and the Ngāpuhi chief Ruatara
journeys.text: Sailing on the brig Active with Ruatara, who had stayed with him at Parramatta, Marsden preached the first Christian sermon in New Zealand at Oihi on Christmas Day 1814, with Ruatara interpreting.

journeys.title: Krapf and Rebmann in East Africa (1844–1849)
journeys.people: Johann Ludwig Krapf and Johannes Rebmann
journeys.text: Krapf reached Mombasa via Zanzibar in 1844; joined by Rebmann in 1846 he founded Rabai. Rebmann's report of snow on Kilimanjaro (11 May 1848) and Krapf's sighting of Mount Kenya from Kitui (December 1849) were ridiculed in Europe before being confirmed.

journeys.title: The first CMS party to Buganda (1876–1877)
journeys.people: Lt George Shergold Smith, C. T. Wilson, Alexander Mackay and others
journeys.text: Responding to Stanley's appeal, CMS sent eight men in 1876; disease and violence reduced them quickly, but Smith and Wilson crossed Lake Victoria to reach Mutesa's court in June 1877. Smith was killed on Ukerewe island months later; Mackay reached Buganda in 1878.

journeys.title: Bishop Hannington's fatal journey to Buganda (1885)
journeys.people: James Hannington with porters from the coast
journeys.text: Hannington took a new northern route through Maasai country, which the Baganda feared as the 'back door' of invasion. Detained at Lubwa's in Busoga, he was killed with most of his porters on Kabaka Mwanga's orders on 29 October 1885.

relations.text: The treatment of Crowther and African clergy in 1887–91 prompted African-led secessions such as the United Native African Church (1891) and fed the wider African church movement.
CMS leaders played major roles at Edinburgh 1910 and in the International Missionary Council; Max Warren was a key IMC figure.
The Cambridge Seven and student volunteer movements of the 1880s supplied CMS with a wave of university recruits.

agreements.text: Venn and the American Board's Rufus Anderson independently formulated the same three-self goal for mission churches.
Shared evangelical theology and anti-slavery commitments, and cooperated in East and Central Africa and India.

disagreements.text: CMS was founded partly because Anglicans could not accept the LMS's undenominational approach, and the two clashed over Madagascar (1864–74).
CMS resisted African secessions and independent churches and disciplined clergy and members who joined them, even while its own policies had provoked them.
Evangelical Anglicans in India rejected the Lutheran toleration of caste distinctions in church, insisting that converts sit and take communion together.

deviations: Venn's goal of handing churches to indigenous leaders was abandoned in the 1880s–90s, when European missionaries took over the Niger Mission and appointed white bishops.
A society founded to evangelise became deeply involved in imperial politics, notably in lobbying for Uganda's annexation.
Keswick-influenced missionaries of the 1880s imposed standards of holiness and racial assumptions that departed from Venn's respect for African agency.
